Chapter 15. The Courage to See Differently.
If you really listen to these stories, there's a quiet theme running through them—the courage it takes to see the world in a whole new way.
It's never easy, is it? Questioning old assumptions, stepping outside what's comfortable, or daring to look at things from a fresh perspective. But you know what? That's exactly where real growth begins.
Picture a student, struggling in school, being told over and over that she'll never make it. At first, she believes it. But then, one caring teacher encourages her to see herself differently.
With a little bit of support, she starts to try new things. She takes risks. She lets herself imagine a different future—one where success is possible.
Or think about a manager in an office, facing a project that everyone has written off as a lost cause. Most people say, "It's doomed." But this manager asks, "What if we tried something new?"
The team pushes back at first, but slowly, they start to notice new opportunities. The project doesn't magically fix itself—but things turn around, all because someone was brave enough to see what everyone else missed.
And then there’s a whole community, hit hard by job losses, families struggling, hope slipping away. Most folks want to give up, but a handful of people ask, "What if we worked together instead?"
It doesn’t happen overnight, but little by little, change takes root. The community starts to rebuild—not because the problems just vanish, but because a few people found the courage to picture a better future.
These stories remind us—seeing differently really does take courage. It means letting go of certainty, stepping away from comfort, and being willing to leave the familiar behind.
Most of us don’t like change, right? But those who lean into it, who open themselves to new possibilities, are the ones who find the future waiting for them.
So, what’s the real secret? The world doesn’t change just because of grand gestures. Most of the time, it’s the small acts of courage that make a difference—people willing to ask new questions, try new things, and notice possibilities others overlook.
